planting.note: Divide rhizomes or plant container-grown specimens in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade.

directions: Plant rhizomes or container-grown specimens in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade; this KwaZulu-Natal and Eastern Cape forest endemic is the shade specialist among the African irises, thriving on the dim floor of mistbelt and coastal forest where its wide, leathery, dark-green fans and unusually large white flowers with soft apricot throat markings stand out against the gloom. Individual blooms open for only a day but are followed in rapid succession by large, prominently ridged seed capsules that persist attractively on the stem and readily self-sow when conditions suit. Keep soil consistently moist and enriched with leaf mold or compost, since this species is far less drought-tolerant than its sun-loving relatives D. iridioides and D. grandiflora and resents prolonged dryness. An excellent choice for woodland gardens, shaded courtyards, and the deep shade beneath live oaks where few other iris relatives will perform.

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in humus-rich soil that stays reliably moist to wet, ideally at a pond margin or stream bank.

directions: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in humus-rich soil that stays reliably moist to wet, ideally at a pond margin, stream bank, or low spot that receives regular irrigation; unlike most Cape moraeas that demand bone-dry summer dormancy, this Drakensberg mountain-stream species is evergreen and keeps its long, arching, strap-like leaf growing through the year, only slowing in the coldest months. Sweetly fragrant, bright golden-yellow flowers with deeper yellow and brown nectar guides open in succession on branching stems that rise well above the foliage from late spring into summer, drawing bees and other pollinators. Coming from high, cold-winter elevations, it tolerates considerably more cold and considerably more moisture than typical winter-rainfall moraeas, making it a rare option for gardeners with a damp or boggy full-sun bed who still want true iris-relative flowers. Divide congested clumps in early spring as new growth resumes.

planting.note: Plant corms 3 inches deep in fertile, moisture-retentive soil in full sun, such as a grassland-style bed or rain-garden margin.

directions: Plant corms 3 inches deep in fertile, moisture-retentive soil in full sun, in a grassland-style bed, damp meadow planting, or the margin of a rain garden; large yellow moraea forms sturdy clumps of a single long, twisted, dark-green leaf per corm and sends up branched, wiry stems bearing a long succession of large, sweetly scented, golden-yellow flowers marked with deeper yellow nectar guides. Individual flowers last only a day but new buds continue opening over many weeks in late spring and into summer, giving a much longer display than the bloom period of any single flower. Native to high-rainfall grasslands and streambanks from the Eastern Cape to Limpopo, it is more tolerant of summer moisture and heavier soils than the classic winter-rainfall Cape moraeas and appreciates organic mulch and consistent moisture through the growing season rather than the strict dry dormancy those species require. Allow clumps to become congested for showier bloom, dividing only when flowering declines.
